modules.title: Probabilistic theories
modules.doc:
A probabilistic theory is described by its ordered real observables and a certain outcome.

## i. Overview

The observables of a physical system form an ordered real vector space. Positive observables are
those whose measured values are never negative. The certain outcome `1` bounds every observable
up to a multiple and sets the scale of the theory. The order is Archimedean, so no observable is
infinitesimally positive and the certain outcome defines a genuine norm.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory` : ordered real observables with a certain outcome and an Archimedean
  order.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Observable space and certain outcome

## iv. References

sections.text: ## A. Observable space and certain outcome

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory
declarations.doc: An ordered real observable space with a certain outcome and no infinitesimal observables.
declarations.statement:
structure ProbabilisticTheory where
  /-- The real observables. -/
  Observables : Type*
  /-- Observables can be added and subtracted. -/
  [addCommGroup : AddCommGroup Observables]
  /-- The order saying which observables are positive. -/
  [partialOrder : PartialOrder Observables]
  /-- Observables can be scaled by real numbers. -/
  [module : Module ℝ Observables]
  /-- Adding an observable preserves the order. -/
  [isOrderedAddMonoid : IsOrderedAddMonoid Observables]
  /-- Scaling by a nonnegative real preserves the order. -/
  [posSMulMono : PosSMulMono ℝ Observables]
  /-- The certain outcome. -/
  [one : One Observables]
  /-- The certain outcome is nonnegative. -/
  one_nonneg' : 0 ≤ (1 : Observables)
  /-- Every observable is bounded above by a natural multiple of the certain outcome. -/
  exists_nsmul_one_le' : ∀ B : Observables, ∃ n : ℕ, B ≤ n • (1 : Observables)
  /-- An observable below every positive multiple of the certain outcome is nonpositive. -/
  le_zero_of_forall_pos_smul_one_le' : ∀ A : Observables,
    (∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → A ≤ ε • (1 : Observables)) → A ≤ 0

modules.title: Positive unital maps
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

In the order-unit-space model used here, a channel is a positive unital transformation: it sends
observables to observables without turning a possible outcome negative, and it leaves the certain
outcome certain. This covers time evolution, noise, and measurements whose outcomes are discarded
at the level of a general probabilistic theory. For quantum systems with a specified composite
structure, physical channels normally require the stronger condition of complete positivity,
which is not expressible using the order-unit structure alone.

A channel `Φ : Channel P Q` between probabilistic theories is a unital positive linear map from
`P.Observables` to `Q.Observables`. States and local nets still use unital positive linear maps
between bare order-unit spaces.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap` : a positive linear map preserving `1`, notated `E →ₚ₁[R] F`.
- `PositiveLinearMap` scalar action : positive linear maps can be scaled by nonnegative reals.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ofLinearMap` : bundle a linear map after checking positivity and
  unitality.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ofPositiveLinearMap` : bundle a positive linear map after checking
  unitality.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.id`, `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.comp` : the identity and composition of
  unital positive linear maps.
- `Channel` : channels between probabilistic theories.
- `Channel.id`, `Channel.comp` : the identity and composition of channels.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Unital positive linear maps
- B. Constructing unital positive linear maps
- C. Scaling positive linear maps
- D. Channels between probabilistic theories

## iv. References

sections.text: ## B. Constructing unital positive linear maps

## C. Scaling positive linear maps

Positive linear maps are closed under addition and under scaling by nonnegative reals, but
unital ones are not closed under scaling.

modules.title: Covariant channels
modules.doc:
Channels that commute with two group actions by reversible transformations.

## i. Overview

More general channels may lose information but can still respect the symmetries of a system. This
is captured by covariance: a channel `Φ` between two spaces carrying group actions `ρ` and `σ` by
reversible transformations is covariant, or intertwining, if

`Φ ∘ ρ g = σ g ∘ Φ` for every group element `g`.

Covariance preserves invariant states under pullback. A reversible transformation is covariant
exactly when the target action is the transport of the source action. Together with the reversible
transformations, this gives a common framework for symmetries and dynamics of observable spaces.

## ii. Key results

- `IsIntertwining`: Covariance of a channel under two group actions.
- `IsIntertwining.comap_isInvariant`: Pullback of invariant states along covariant channels.
- `Reversible.isIntertwining_iff_eq_transport`: Characterization of the transported action.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Covariant channels
  - A.1. Definition and closure properties
  - A.2. Invariant states
- B. Covariance of transport

## iv. References

modules.title: Channels are contractions
modules.doc:
Unital positive linear maps are contractions with respect to the order-unit norm and are
therefore continuous.

## i. Overview

The norm bound follows from the characterization of the order-unit norm in terms of states.
Every state on the codomain pulls back along a channel to a state on the domain, so evaluating
the image of an observable cannot exceed its original norm.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.norm_apply_le`: Channels are contractions.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.continuous`: Channels are continuous.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toContinuousLinearMap`: Channels as continuous linear maps.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Contractivity and continuity

## iv. References

modules.title: Reversible transformations of observables
modules.doc:
Reversible transformations of observable spaces, their group structure, their action on states and
the transport of group actions.

## i. Overview

Time evolution, spatial symmetries and changes of reference frame all have something in common:
they transform observables in a way that can be undone.

This motivates reversible transformations, defined as unital linear order isomorphisms of
observable spaces. They form a group and naturally act on states. A group representation by
reversible transformations describes symmetries or reversible dynamics. For example, time evolution
is represented by the additive group of real numbers. A reversible transformation also transports a
group action from one observable space to another by conjugation.

## ii. Key results

- `Reversible`: Reversible transformations, i.e. unital linear order isomorphisms of
  observable spaces.
- `Reversible.toChannelHom`: Reversible transformations embed in the monoid of channels.
- `Reversible.instMulActionState`: The induced action on states.
- `Reversible.transport`: Transport of a group action along a reversible transformation.
- `IsInvariant`: A state fixed by every transformation of a group action.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Reversible transformations
  - A.1. Definition
  - A.2. Group structure
  - A.3. As channels
- B. Action on states
- C. Transport of group actions
  - C.1. Conjugation
  - C.2. Transported actions
- D. Invariant states

## iv. References

modules.title: The observables of a C⋆-algebra
modules.doc:
The self-adjoint part of a unital C⋆-algebra is an Archimedean order-unit space.

## i. Overview

The observables of a quantum system are the self-adjoint elements of its C⋆-algebra. One
observable lies below another if their difference has no negative measurement outcome. The
identity is the certain outcome.

Every observable lies below a multiple of the identity. So no outcome exceeds the norm.

An observable that lies below every positive multiple of the identity has no positive outcome.
This is the Archimedean property.

## ii. Key results

- `selfAdjoint.le_nsmul_one_ceil_norm` : every observable lies below a natural multiple of the
  identity.
- `selfAdjoint.le_zero_of_forall_pos_smul_one_le` : an element below every positive multiple of
  the identity is below zero.
- `selfAdjoint.instOrderUnitSpace` : the observables form an order-unit space.
- `selfAdjoint.instArchimedeanOrderUnitSpace` : it is Archimedean.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The order-unit space of observables
- B. The Archimedean property

## iv. References

modules.title: Effects
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

An effect models a yes/no measurement outcome, ranging continuously between the impossible
outcome `0` and the certain outcome `1`. Formally, it is a point of the order interval `[0, 1]`
inside `E`. For self-adjoint matrices, effects are exactly the operators `0 ≤ M ≤ 1` — the
elements of a POVM.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect` : a bounded measurement outcome, the order interval `[0, 1]`.
- `Effect.mem_iff_mem_posCone_and_one_sub_mem_posCone` : an effect is exactly a positive element
  whose complement from the order unit is also positive.
- `Effect.exists_pos_smul_mem` : every positive observable becomes an effect after scaling it down
  enough.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Effects

## iv. References

- G. Ludwig, *Foundations of Quantum Mechanics I*, Springer, 1983.
  <https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-86751-4>

lemma exists_pos_smul_mem {B : E} (hB : 0 ≤ B) :
    ∃ r : ℝ, 0 < r ∧ r • B ∈ Effect E

modules.title: Complementary effects
modules.doc:
The complement `1 - e` of an effect, its antitonicity and compatibility with mixtures.

## i. Overview

The complement of an effect `e` is the yes/no test that fires exactly when `e` doesn't: `1 - e`.
Physically, a state's probability of "no" is always `1` minus its probability of "yes".

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.complement` : the complementary effect `1 - e`.
- `Effect.complement_antitone` : the complement reverses order.
- `Effect.complement_mix` : the complement of a mixture is the mixture of the complements.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The complement
- B. Monotonicity of the complement
- C. The complement and mixtures

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.coe_complement

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.complement_complement

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.complement_antitone
declarations.doc: The complement reverses order: a more certain test's complement is a less certain one.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.complement_one

modules.title: Convexity and mixtures of effects
modules.doc:
The effect interval is convex, so effects can be mixed with a given probability.

## i. Overview

The effect interval `[0, 1]` is convex: randomizing between two effects with some probability
gives back an effect. Physically, flipping a biased coin to decide which of two measurements to
actually run is itself a legitimate measurement.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.convex` : the effect interval is convex.
- `Effect.mix` : randomize between two effects with a given probability.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Convexity and mixtures of effects

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.statement: lemma convex : Convex ℝ (Effect E)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.mix
declarations.doc: Randomize between two effects with probability `t` of testing the first.

modules.title: The metric space of effects
modules.doc:
The order-unit metric on effects and their identification with the order-unit-norm ball.

## i. Overview

Effects sit inside `E`, so pulling back the order-unit norm along the inclusion `Effect E ↪ E`
gives them a metric space structure for free.

Effects also correspond to points of the order-unit-norm ball, by the affine rescaling
`e ↦ 2 • e - 1` that turns `[0, 1]` into the symmetric `[-1, 1]` the norm itself ranges over.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.dist_eq_orderUnitNorm` : the effect metric is the order-unit norm of the difference.
- `Effect.effectEquiv` : effects correspond to points of the order-unit-norm ball.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The effect metric
- B. Effects as points of the order-unit-norm ball

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.orderUnitNorm_two_smul_sub_one_le_one
declarations.doc: Doubling and re-centering an effect at the order unit lands in the order-unit-norm ball.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_two_smul_sub_one_le_one (e : Effect E) :
    orderUnitNorm (2 • (e : E) - 1) ≤ 1

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.mem_effect_two_inv_smul_one_add
declarations.doc: Undoing the re-centering on a point of the order-unit-norm ball gives back an effect.
declarations.statement:

    (2 : ℝ)⁻¹ • (1 + A) ∈ Effect E

    (2 : ℝ)⁻¹ • (1 + (2 • (e : E) - 1)) = (e : E)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.two_smul_two_inv_smul_one_add_sub_one
declarations.doc: Undoing the re-centering, then redoing it, returns the original ball point.
declarations.statement:
lemma two_smul_two_inv_smul_one_add_sub_one (A : E) :
    2 • ((2 : ℝ)⁻¹ • (1 + A)) - 1 = A

declarations.doc:
Effects correspond to points of the order-unit-norm ball by doubling and re-centering at the
order unit: `e ↦ 2 • e - 1`, with inverse `A ↦ (1 + A) / 2`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def effectEquiv : Effect E ≃ {A : E // orderUnitNorm A ≤ 1}

modules.title: Sharp effects
modules.doc:
Sharp effects: extreme points of the effect interval, preserved by taking complements.

## i. Overview

The effect interval `[0, 1]` is convex. A sharp effect is an extreme point of it: one that cannot
be written as a nontrivial mixture of two distinct effects. Sharp effects generalize projections.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.IsSharp` : an effect that cannot be written as a nontrivial mixture of two distinct
  effects.
- `Effect.isSharp_complement_iff` : sharpness is preserved by taking the complement.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Sharp effects

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: Local nets of observables
modules.doc:
Observables of subsystems and their inclusion into larger subsystems.

## i. Overview

Let `R` index subsystems, with `X ≤ Y` meaning that `X` is contained in `Y`. The observables of
`X` form an order-unit space `A X`. A local net assigns to `X ≤ Y` a channel,
which regards an observable of `X` as one of `Y`.

For a tensor product system with `H_Y ≃ H_X ⊗ H_rest`, take `A X` to be the Hermitian operators
on `H_X`. Then the inclusion is the familiar map `M ↦ M ⊗ 1`: the observable acts as `M` on `X` and
as the identity on the remaining factors.

The local observables can also be viewed in one space, `N.Quasilocal`, the algebraic direct limit
of the local observable spaces. It is a real vector space and carries no norm. Completing it in a
norm, which needs more structure than is assumed here, gives the quasilocal algebra of the physics
literature. Inductive limits of order-unit spaces are developed in [ref: arxiv_1705_04663].

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet`: subsystem observables with channels into larger subsystems.
- `LocalNet.IsOrderEmbedding`: the inclusion maps reflect order.
- `LocalNet.map_le_map_iff`: inclusion preserves and reflects inequalities.
- `LocalNet.incl_injective`: order-embedding inclusion maps are injective.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal`: the algebraic direct limit of the local observable spaces.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal`: regard an observable of one subsystem as a quasilocal observable.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_iff`: equality of quasilocal observables can be checked in a common
  larger subsystem.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal_injective`: order-embedding inclusions keep local observables distinct.
- `LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq`, `exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂`: quasilocal observables have
  representatives in a single subsystem, and any two have representatives in a common one.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Subsystems and inclusions
- B. Order-embedding inclusions
- C. The quasilocal observable space
- D. Embedding the local observables
- E. Directed families of subsystems

## iv. References

* L. Mawhinney, I. G. Todorov, *Inductive limits in the operator system and related categories*,
  arXiv:1705.04663. [ref: arxiv_1705_04663]

sections.text:
## C. The quasilocal observable space

For a directed family of subsystems, observables from different subsystems can be included in a
common larger one and combined there. The direct limit identifies all such local descriptions
consistently and supplies the resulting real vector space.

## D. Embedding the local observables

The map `toQuasilocal N i` takes an observable of subsystem `i` to the quasilocal observable it
represents.

## E. Directed families of subsystems

If any two subsystems are contained in a common larger one, the quasilocal observable space is
described by representatives in single subsystems.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet
declarations.doc: The observables of each subsystem, with channels into larger subsystems.
declarations.statement:
structure LocalNet (R : Type*) [Preorder R] (A : R → Type*)
    [∀ X, OrderUnitSpace (A X)] where
  /-- Regard an observable of `X` as an observable of `Y` when `X ≤ Y`. -/
  incl : ∀ {X Y : R}, X ≤ Y → A X →ₚ₁[ℝ] A Y
  /-- Inclusion into the same subsystem is the identity. -/
  incl_refl : ∀ X : R, incl (le_refl X) = .id ℝ (A X)
  /-- Including through an intermediate subsystem agrees with direct inclusion. -/
  incl_trans : ∀ {X Y Z : R} (h₁ : X ≤ Y) (h₂ : Y ≤ Z) (h₃ : X ≤ Z),
    incl h₃ = (incl h₂).comp (incl h₁)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_refl_apply
declarations.doc: An observable is unchanged by inclusion into the same subsystem.
declarations.statement: lemma incl_refl_apply (X : R) (a : A X) : N.incl (le_refl X) a = a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_trans_apply
declarations.doc: Including an observable through an intermediate subsystem agrees with direct inclusion.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_trans_apply (h₁ : X ≤ Y) (h₂ : Y ≤ Z) (h₃ : X ≤ Z) (a : A X) :
    N.incl h₃ a = N.incl h₂ (N.incl h₁ a)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.IsOrderEmbedding
declarations.doc: The inclusion maps are order embeddings if each reflects positivity.
declarations.statement:
class IsOrderEmbedding (N : LocalNet R A) : Prop where
  /-- An observable that is positive in a larger subsystem is already positive in the smaller. -/
  nonneg_of_incl_nonneg : ∀ {X Y : R} (h : X ≤ Y) {a : A X}, 0 ≤ N.incl h a → 0 ≤ a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.map_le_map_iff
declarations.doc: Inclusion in an order-embedding net preserves and reflects inequalities.
declarations.statement:
lemma map_le_map_iff [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (h : X ≤ Y) {a b : A X} :
    N.incl h a ≤ N.incl h b ↔ a ≤ b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_injective
declarations.doc: The inclusion maps of an order-embedding net are injective.
declarations.statement: lemma incl_injective [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (h : X ≤ Y) : Function.Injective (N.incl h)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.inclLin
declarations.doc:
The inclusions as linear maps: the transition maps of the direct limit defining
`N.Quasilocal`.
declarations.statement: abbrev inclLin (N : LocalNet R A) ⦃X Y : R⦄ (h : X ≤ Y) : A X →ₗ[ℝ] A Y

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.directedSystem
declarations.doc:
The inclusions form a directed system: including a subsystem into itself does nothing, and
successive inclusions compose.
declarations.statement: instance directedSystem (N : LocalNet R A) : DirectedSystem A fun _ _ h => N.inclLin h

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.Quasilocal
declarations.doc: The algebraic direct limit of the local observable spaces.
declarations.statement: def Quasilocal (N : LocalNet R A) : Type _

declarations.doc: Quasilocal observables add, as elements of a direct limit of vector spaces.
declarations.statement: noncomputable instance : AddCommGroup N.Quasilocal

declarations.doc: Quasilocal observables can be scaled by real numbers.
declarations.statement: noncomputable instance : Module ℝ N.Quasilocal

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal
declarations.doc: Regard an observable of subsystem `i` as a quasilocal observable.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def toQuasilocal (i : R) : A i →ₗ[ℝ] N.Quasilocal

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_incl
declarations.doc: Including an observable in a larger subsystem does not change its quasilocal representation.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_incl {i j : R} (h : i ≤ j) (a : A i) :
    toQuasilocal N j (N.incl h a) = toQuasilocal N i a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_of_incl_eq
declarations.doc:
Observables that agree in a common larger subsystem represent the same quasilocal
observable.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_eq_of_incl_eq {i j k : R} (hik : i ≤ k) (hjk : j ≤ k) {a : A i} {b : A j}
    (h : N.incl hik a = N.incl hjk b) : toQuasilocal N i a = toQuasilocal N j b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_incl_eq_of_toQuasilocal_eq
declarations.doc:
Observables representing the same quasilocal observable agree in a common larger
subsystem.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_iff
declarations.doc:
Two local observables represent the same quasilocal observable exactly when they agree in a
common larger subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_eq_iff {i j : R} (a : A i) (b : A j) :
    toQuasilocal N i a = toQuasilocal N j b ↔
      ∃ (k : R) (hik : i ≤ k) (hjk : j ≤ k), N.incl hik a = N.incl hjk b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_injective
declarations.doc: Order-embedding inclusions keep distinct local observables distinct in the quasilocal space.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_injective [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (i : R) :
    Function.Injective (toQuasilocal N i)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq
declarations.doc: Every quasilocal observable has a representative in some subsystem.
declarations.statement: lemma exists_toQuasilocal_eq (x : N.Quasilocal) : ∃ (i : R) (a : A i), toQuasilocal N i a = x

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂
declarations.doc: Any two quasilocal observables have representatives in a common subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂ (x y : N.Quasilocal) :
    ∃ (i : R) (a b : A i), toQuasilocal N i a = x ∧ toQuasilocal N i b = y

modules.title: Interactions on a local net
modules.doc:
An interaction is a family of local observables, each associated with a region of the net.

## i. Overview

Extensive observables such as energy, magnetization and particle number can be expressed as
sums of local terms. An interaction assigns a supporting region and an observable to each
label. Each term can be included into any larger region and is taken to be zero when its
support is not contained in the region.

## ii. Key results

- `Interaction`: A family of local observables with specified supports.
- `Interaction.termIn`: An interaction term expressed in a given region.
- `Interaction.incl_termIn`: Compatibility with inclusions of regions.
- `Interaction.termIn_add`: Compatibility with addition.
- `Interaction.termIn_smul`: Compatibility with scalar multiplication.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Interactions
- B. Interaction terms in a region

## iv. References

sections.text: ## B. Interaction terms in a region

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction
declarations.doc: A family of local observables on `N`, indexed by `ι`, with specified supports.
declarations.statement:
structure Interaction (N : LocalNet R A) (ι : Type*) where
  /-- The supporting region of each term. -/
  supp : ι → R
  /-- The observable associated with each term. -/
  term : ∀ i, A (supp i)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.labelsIn
declarations.doc: The labels of terms supported in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: def labelsIn (Λ : R) : Set ι

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn
declarations.doc: The term `i` expressed in `Λ`, or zero if its support is not contained in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def termIn (Λ : R) (i : ι) : A Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.incl_termIn
declarations.doc:
Including a term from `Λ` into `Λ'` agrees with evaluating it in `Λ'` whenever
its support is contained in `Λ`, and gives zero otherwise.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_termIn {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (i : ι) :
    N.incl h (Φ.termIn Λ i) = (Φ.labelsIn Λ).indicator (Φ.termIn Λ') i

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn_add
declarations.doc: Evaluating interaction terms in a region preserves addition.
declarations.statement:
lemma termIn_add (s : ι → R) (t t' : ∀ i, A (s i)) (Λ : R) (i : ι) :
    (⟨s, t + t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i =
      (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i +
        (⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn_smul
declarations.doc: Evaluating interaction terms in a region preserves scalar multiplication.
declarations.statement:
lemma termIn_smul (s : ι → R) (c : ℝ) (t : ∀ i, A (s i)) (Λ : R) (i : ι) :
    (⟨s, c • t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i =
      c • (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i

modules.title: Integrating interactions over local regions
modules.doc:
An interaction defines a local observable by integrating its terms over a region.

## i. Overview

The integral of an interaction gives an observable in each region. The choice of measure allows
both discrete sums and continuum integrals.

For nested regions, the observable in the larger region decomposes into the observable of the
smaller region and the remaining interaction terms. For two regions with disjoint sets of
supported terms, the observable decomposes into their contributions and the terms supported
in neither region.

## ii. Key results

- `Interaction.sumIn`: The integral of interaction terms in a region.
- `Interaction.norm_sumIn_le`: A norm bound for the integral.
- `Interaction.sumIn_add`, `Interaction.sumIn_smul`: Linearity of integration.
- `Interaction.sumIn_split`: Decomposition for nested regions.
- `Interaction.sumIn_disjoint`: Decomposition for regions with disjoint sets of terms.
- `Interaction.sumIn_count`, `Interaction.sumIn_count_tsum`: Discrete sums over finite or
  countable labels.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Integration over a region
- B. Nested regions
- C. Disjoint regions
- D. Discrete interactions

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.norm_termIn_le
declarations.doc: The norm of a term cannot increase when included into another region.
declarations.statement: lemma norm_termIn_le (Λ : R) (i : ι) : ‖Φ.termIn Λ i‖ ≤ ‖Φ.term i‖

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn
declarations.doc: The observable in `Λ` obtained by integrating the interaction terms supported there.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def sumIn (Λ : R) : A Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.norm_sumIn_le
declarations.doc: The norm of the integral is bounded by the integral of the norms.
declarations.statement: lemma norm_sumIn_le (Λ : R) : ‖Φ.sumIn μ Λ‖ ≤ ∫ i, ‖Φ.termIn Λ i‖ ∂μ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_add
declarations.doc: Integration preserves addition of interaction terms with the same supports.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_add (s : ι → R) (t t' : ∀ i, A (s i)) {Λ : R}
    (h : Integrable ((⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ) μ)
    (h' : Integrable ((⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ) μ) :
    (⟨s, t + t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ =
      (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ + (⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_smul
declarations.doc: Integration preserves scalar multiplication of interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_smul (s : ι → R) (c : ℝ) (t : ∀ i, A (s i)) (Λ : R) :
    (⟨s, c • t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ =
      c • (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.setIntegral_labelsIn
declarations.doc:
Integrating the terms supported in `Λ` in a larger region `Λ'` agrees with including
the integral over `Λ` into `Λ'`.
declarations.statement:
lemma setIntegral_labelsIn {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (hS : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ))
    (h1 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ) μ) :
    ∫ i in Φ.labelsIn Λ, Φ.termIn Λ' i ∂μ = N.incl h (Φ.sumIn μ Λ)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.coupling
declarations.doc: The contribution in `Λ'` from terms not supported in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def coupling (Λ Λ' : R) : A Λ'

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_split
declarations.doc:
The observable in a larger region is the included observable of the smaller region
plus the remaining interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_split {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (hS : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ))
    (h1 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ) μ) (h2 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ') μ) :
    Φ.sumIn μ Λ' = N.incl h (Φ.sumIn μ Λ) + Φ.coupling μ Λ Λ'

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.crossingIn
declarations.doc: The contribution in `Λ` from terms supported in neither `Λ₁` nor `Λ₂`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def crossingIn (Λ₁ Λ₂ Λ : R) : A Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_disjoint
declarations.doc:
For regions with disjoint sets of supported terms, the observable in a common larger
region is the sum of their included observables and the remaining interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_disjoint {Λ₁ Λ₂ Λ : R} (h₁ : Λ₁ ≤ Λ) (h₂ : Λ₂ ≤ Λ)
    (hd : Disjoint (Φ.labelsIn Λ₁) (Φ.labelsIn Λ₂)) (m₁ : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ₁))
    (m₂ : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ₂)) (g₁ : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ₁) μ)

modules.title: Order-unit structure on quasilocal observables
modules.doc:
Positivity and a common unit for observables assembled from a local net.

## i. Overview

The quasilocal construction treats observables from different subsystems as observables of one
global system. A quantity measured locally can also be described in a larger subsystem; these
descriptions must refer to the same physical quantity. For the global description to work, it must
preserve more than identity: whether an observable is positive, how it compares with other
observables, and what represents the certain outcome.

This file shows how those properties carry over from the local systems. Positive local observables
give the quasilocal space its notion of positivity, and the local copies of `1` give it one certain
observable. Local observables thereby retain their interpretation as observables of the whole
system. The resulting order-unit structure lets a state of the global system assign positive,
normalized expectations to them.

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.positive`: the global observables with a positive local representative.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.toQuasilocal_nonneg_iff`: local and global positivity agree when inclusions
  reflect order.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.instOrderUnitSpace`: the global observables inherit an order unit.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.toQuasilocalChannel`: each subsystem maps to the global observable space
  by a channel.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.instArchimedeanOrderUnitSpace`: the global space is Archimedean when the
  local spaces are.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Positivity
- B. The common order unit
- C. The order
- D. The quasilocal order-unit space and local channels
- E. The Archimedean property

## iv. References

sections.text:
## A. Positivity

An observable assembled from local pieces is positive when it has a positive local description.
Positive observables from different subsystems can be brought into a common larger subsystem and
added there. Nonnegative scaling preserves positivity within any one subsystem.

## B. The common order unit

The certain observable must not depend on which subsystem describes it. Every inclusion preserves
`1`, so the local units all represent one global observable.

## C. The order

A comparison `x ≤ y` means that `y - x` has a positive local description. This is a partial order:
an observable cannot be both positive and negative unless it is zero. When inclusions reflect
order, comparisons made within a subsystem agree with comparisons in the global system.

## D. The quasilocal order-unit space and local channels

Every global observable has a local representative bounded by a multiple of the local unit. The
same bound holds for the global unit, making it an order unit. The map from each subsystem to the
global space preserves positivity and `1`, so it is a channel.

## E. The Archimedean property

The global description should not introduce infinitesimal observables absent from every local
system. This property can be checked on a local representative, so it passes to the quasilocal
space.

modules.title: Archimedean order-unit spaces
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

The Archimedean condition is a regularity assumption on an order-unit space that rules out
infinitesimal elements. With it, the order and the distinguished unit `1` determine a natural
norm,

`‖A‖₁ = inf {r ≥ 0 | -r • 1 ≤ A ≤ r • 1}`.

Thus the unit interval sets the scale of the theory: `[-1, 1]` is exactly the closed unit ball. For
self-adjoint matrices, this recovers the usual operator norm. Concretely, this is the Minkowski
functional of the order interval `[-1, 1]`: convexity of that interval gives the triangle
inequality, and its symmetry gives homogeneity, for free. The Archimedean condition is only needed
afterwards, to upgrade this from a seminorm to a genuine norm.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.instArchimedeanOrderUnitSpace` : the observables of a probabilistic theory
  form an Archimedean order-unit space.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.of` : an Archimedean order-unit space regarded as a probabilistic theory.
- `ArchimedeanOrderUnitSpace.orderUnitNorm_eq_zero_iff` : the order-unit norm separates points.
- `ArchimedeanOrderUnitSpace.closedIciTopology` : the positive cone is closed in the order-unit-norm
  topology.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Archimedean order units
- B. The order-unit bounds and norm
- C. Norm axioms
- D. The induced normed space
- E. Order-closedness of the topology

## iv. References

modules.title: Ordered vector spaces and order units
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Order-unit spaces capture the basic structure needed for a probabilistic theory: observables,
positivity, effects, states and probabilities. They do this without assuming that the theory is
classical or quantum, or that observables have any particular algebraic structure.

In quantum mechanics, the standard example is the real vector space of self-adjoint matrices,
ordered by positive semidefiniteness, with the identity matrix as 1. Keeping only the vector
space, its order, and this distinguished unit gives the abstract order-unit setting.

## ii. Key results

- `OrderUnitSpace.exists_two_sided_bound` : every observable sits between `-(n • 1)` and `n • 1`,
  for some `n`.
- `OrderUnitSpace.exists_eq_sub_nonneg` : every observable is a difference of two positive
  observables.
- `OrderUnitSpace.exists_real_shift_nonneg` : enough copies of the order unit shift any element
  into the positive cone.
- `OrderedVectorSpace.nonneg_add_eq_zero` : the positive cone meets its negation only at `0`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Ordered vector spaces and order units
- B. Consequences of being an order unit

## iv. References

## i. Overview

`PosCone E` collects the positive elements of `E`. In quantum mechanics, `E` is the real vector
space of self-adjoint matrices, whose spectra are real. Its positive cone consists exactly of
those matrices whose spectra are nonnegative.
These elements form a cone: they are closed under addition and scaling by nonnegative reals.

## ii. Key results

- `PosCone` : the cone of positive observables, `PointedCone.positive ℝ E`. Its carrier is exactly
  `{A | 0 ≤ A}` (`PointedCone.mem_positive`) and it is convex (`PointedCone.convex`).
- `PosCone.isClosed` : the positive cone is closed in the order-unit-norm topology of an
  Archimedean order-unit space.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The positive cone
- B. Topological closedness
- C. The order unit

modules.title: Observables and states of a star algebra
modules.doc:
A positive map sends observables to observables. A state gives observables real expectation
values. A tracial state does not see the order of a product.

## i. Overview

The observables of a quantum system are the self-adjoint operators of its algebra. A state gives
every operator a complex expectation value.

A state is tracial if the expectation value of a product does not depend on the order of the
factors: `ω (a b) = ω (b a)`. Then `ω` vanishes on every commutator. A tracial state gives the
same expectation value after a change of frame by a unitary `u`: `ω (u x u⋆) = ω x`.

A state has a real expectation value on every observable. Its real part is a state of the
observables.

A positive map sends the operators of one system to operators of another. It sends observables to
observables. A unital positive map restricts to a channel between the observables.

## ii. Key results

- `Observable` : the self-adjoint elements, such as Hermitian operators.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsTracial` : a tracial state.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsTracial.map_commutator` : a tracial state vanishes on commutators.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsTracial.map_conj` : a tracial state is invariant under
  `x ↦ u * x * u⋆` for a unitary `u`.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isTracial_iff_star_mul_self_eq_mul_star_self` : `ω` is tracial if and
  only if `ω (a⋆ * a) = ω (a * a⋆)` for all `a`.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.onObservables` : a state restricted to a state of the observables.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.coe_onObservables_apply` : the expectation value of an observable is
  real.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.restrictObservables` : a unital positive map restricted to a channel
  between observables.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Observables and tracial states
- B. States of observables
- C. Channels between observables

## iv. References

modules.title: Tracial functionals
modules.doc:
A functional on an algebra is tracial if the order of a product does not change its value.

## i. Overview

A functional `f` on an algebra is tracial if `f (x y) = f (y x)` for all `x` and `y`. The order
of a product does not change its value.

On an algebra with an adjoint it is enough to check `f (x⋆ x) = f (x x⋆)`. An operator and its
adjoint then give the same value in both orders.

## ii. Key results

- `LinearMap.IsTracial` : a complex-linear functional with `f (x * y) = f (y * x)`.
- `LinearMap.isTracial_iff_star_mul_self_eq_mul_star_self` : `f` is tracial if and only if
  `f (x⋆ * x) = f (x * x⋆)` for all `x`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Tracial functionals
- B. Checking on `x⋆ x`

## iv. References

sections.text:
## B. Checking on `x⋆ x`

Apply the hypothesis to `x⋆ + y` and `x⋆ + i y`. The cross terms leave `C - C' = 0` and
`C + C' = 0` for the commutators `C = f [x, y]` and `C' = f [x⋆, y⋆]`, so `C = 0`.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsTracial
declarations.doc: A complex-linear functional is tracial if `f (x * y) = f (y * x)` for all `x` and `y`.
declarations.statement: def IsTracial (f : 𝒜 →ₗ[ℂ] ℂ) : Prop

declarations.name: LinearMap.isTracial_iff_star_mul_self_eq_mul_star_self
declarations.doc: A functional is tracial if and only if `f (x⋆ x) = f (x x⋆)` for all `x`.
declarations.statement:
lemma isTracial_iff_star_mul_self_eq_mul_star_self (f : 𝒜 →ₗ[ℂ] ℂ) :
    f.IsTracial ↔ ∀ x : 𝒜, f (star x * x) = f (x * star x)

modules.title: States
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

A state assigns each observable its expectation value: a positive linear functional
(`0 ≤ A ⟹ 0 ≤ ω A`), normalized so the certain outcome reads `ω 1 = 1`. In quantum mechanics,
`ω A = tr(ρA)` for a density matrix `ρ`.

## ii. Key results

- `𝓢[𝕜, A]` : states on an ordered `𝕜`-vector space with a distinguished unit.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.comap` : the state on the input of a channel that evaluates an
  observable by first sending it through the channel.
- `Channel.comap` : the same pullback of states along a channel between probabilistic theories.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Notation for positive functionals and states
- B. Transporting states along channels

## iv. References

The state on `E` that evaluates an observable by first sending it through a channel `f` and

modules.title: Convex state spaces
modules.doc:
Convexity of the state space and its pure and mixed states.

## i. Overview

States mix: a probabilistic combination of two states is again a state, and the state space
embeds convexly into the algebraic dual. A pure state is one that's never a genuine mixture of
two others, an extreme point of that convex set. A mixed state is one that is a mixture.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.mix` : randomize between two states with a given probability.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.stateSpace_convex` : the state space is convex in the algebraic dual.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsPure` : pure states are extreme points of the state space.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq` : a pure state admits only trivial
  genuine mixtures.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment` : mixed states lie between
  two other states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Mixing states
- B. The state space
- C. Pure and mixed states

## iv. References

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.mix
declarations.doc:
Randomize between two states with probability `t` of choosing the first, so
`t • ω + σ t • φ` with `σ t = 1 - t`.
declarations.statement: def mix (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (t : unitInterval) : 𝓢[ℝ, E]

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.mix_apply
declarations.doc: Evaluation of a mixture is the pointwise convex combination.
declarations.statement:
lemma mix_apply (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (t : unitInterval) (A : E) :
    mix ω φ t A = (t : ℝ) * ω A + (1 - (t : ℝ)) * φ A

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toLinearMap_mix
declarations.doc: The underlying linear map of a mixture is the corresponding combination of linear maps.
declarations.statement:
lemma toLinearMap_mix (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (t : unitInterval) :
    (mix ω φ t).toLinearMap = (t : ℝ) • ω.toLinearMap + (1 - (t : ℝ)) • φ.toLinearMap

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.mix_symm
declarations.doc: Swapping the two states swaps the weights: `σ` is the symmetry of the interval.
declarations.statement: lemma mix_symm (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (t : unitInterval) : mix ω φ t = mix φ ω (σ t)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.stateSpace
declarations.doc: States embedded into the algebraic dual.
declarations.statement: def stateSpace : Set (E →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.stateSpace_convex
declarations.doc: The state space is convex in the algebraic dual.
declarations.statement: lemma stateSpace_convex : Convex ℝ (stateSpace (E := E))

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsPure
declarations.doc: A state is pure when it is an extreme point of the state space.
declarations.statement: def IsPure (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : Prop

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.IsMixed
declarations.doc: A state is mixed when it isn't pure.
declarations.statement: def IsMixed (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : Prop

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isPure_iff_forall_mem_openSegment
declarations.doc: A state is pure exactly when any open segment containing it has both endpoints equal to it.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPure_iff_forall_mem_openSegment {ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]} :
    ω.IsPure ↔ ∀ φ ψ : 𝓢[ℝ, E],
      ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap → φ = ω ∧ ψ = ω

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment
declarations.doc: A state is mixed exactly when it lies in an open segment with a different endpoint.
declarations.statement:
lemma isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment {ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]} :
    ω.IsMixed ↔ ∃ φ ψ : 𝓢[ℝ, E],
      ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap ∧ (φ ≠ ω ∨ ψ ≠ ω)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.mem_openSegment_iff_exists_mix
declarations.doc: Open segments between states consist exactly of their genuine mixtures.
declarations.statement:
lemma mem_openSegment_iff_exists_mix (ω φ ψ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap ↔
      ∃ t : unitInterval, 0 < t ∧ t < 1 ∧ mix φ ψ t = ω

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq
declarations.doc: A state is pure exactly when every genuine binary mixture producing it is trivial.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq {ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]} :
    ω.IsPure ↔ ∀ φ ψ t, 0 < t → t < 1 → mix φ ψ t = ω → φ = ω ∧ ψ = ω

modules.title: State discrimination
modules.doc:
Optimal binary discrimination probabilities and their relation to the state distance.

## i. Overview

A system is prepared in state `ω₀` (with probability `p`) or `ω₁` (with probability `1 - p`). We
get to run a single yes/no test on it — an effect `e` — and have to guess which state it was,
based only on whether `e` "clicked". We guess `ω₀` on a click and `ω₁` otherwise; `successProb`
is the probability that guess is right.

Always guessing `ω₁`, without even looking at the system, is already right with probability
`1 - p` — that's our baseline. Running a test can only add to it: its `advantage` is how much
extra success probability it buys over that baseline. Taking the supremum over all tests gives the
classic Helstrom bound (`optimalSuccessProb_eq`), without assuming an optimizing test exists.

For equal priors (`p = 1/2`) the bound simplifies to `1/2 + dist ω₀ ω₁ / 4`.
Two equally likely states are easier to tell apart exactly when they sit farther apart.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.optimalSuccessProb_eq` : the Helstrom bound.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq` : for equal priors, the bound is the
  state distance.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Success probability and the advantage of a test
- B. The Helstrom bound
- C. Equal priors: the bound is the state distance

## iv. References

- C.W. Helstrom, *Quantum Detection and Estimation Theory*, Academic Press, 1976.

sections.text: ## A. Success probability and the advantage of a test
## C. Equal priors: the bound is the state distance

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.successProb
declarations.doc:
Probability of guessing right between `ω₀` (prior `p`) and `ω₁` (prior `1 - p`) using test
`e`: guess `ω₀` on a click, `ω₁` otherwise.
declarations.statement: def successProb (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) (e : Effect E) : ℝ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.advantage
declarations.doc: How much test `e` improves on the baseline of always guessing `ω₁`.
declarations.statement: def advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) (e : Effect E) : ℝ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.successProb_eq_add_advantage
declarations.doc: Success probability equals the baseline `1 - p` plus the advantage of test `e`.
declarations.statement:
lemma successProb_eq_add_advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) (e : Effect E) :
    successProb ω₀ ω₁ p e = (1 - p) + advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.advantage_le
declarations.doc: No test's advantage beats the prior weight `p` of the state it favors.
declarations.statement:
lemma advantage_le (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) (e : Effect E) :
    advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e ≤ p

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.bddAbove_advantage
declarations.doc: Advantages of tests are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) :
    BddAbove (Set.range (advantage ω₀ ω₁ p))

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.optimalSuccessProb
declarations.doc: The best a single test can do.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def optimalSuccessProb (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) : ℝ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.optimalSuccessProb_eq
declarations.doc:
The Helstrom bound: optimal success probability is the baseline `1 - p` plus the best
advantage any test can give.
declarations.statement:
lemma optimalSuccessProb_eq (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (p : unitInterval) :
    optimalSuccessProb ω₀ ω₁ p = (1 - p) + ⨆ e : Effect E, advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.sub_complement_eq_neg_sub
declarations.doc: Complementing an effect negates `ω₀ e - ω₁ e`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sub_complement_eq_neg_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (e : Effect E) :
    ω₀ (complement e) - ω₁ (complement e) = -(ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.bddAbove_abs_sub
declarations.doc: The differences `|ω₀ e - ω₁ e|` over effects are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun e : Effect E => |ω₀ e - ω₁ e|)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.bddAbove_sub
declarations.doc: The differences `ω₀ e - ω₁ e` over effects are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun e : Effect E => ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ciSup_sub_eq_ciSup_abs_sub
declarations.doc:
The supremum of the state-value difference equals that of its absolute value: complementing
an effect flips the sign.
declarations.statement:
lemma ciSup_sub_eq_ciSup_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    (⨆ e : Effect E, (ω₀ e - ω₁ e)) = ⨆ e : Effect E, |ω₀ e - ω₁ e|

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_eq_ciSup_abs_sub
declarations.doc: The state distance is the supremum of the differences on recentered effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_eq_ciSup_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    dist ω₀ ω₁ =
      ⨆ e : Effect E, |ω₀ (effectEquiv e) - ω₁ (effectEquiv e)|

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_eq_two_mul_ciSup_sub
declarations.doc: The state distance is twice the largest state-value difference over all effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_eq_two_mul_ciSup_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    dist ω₀ ω₁ = 2 * ⨆ e : Effect E, (ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq
declarations.doc: For equal priors, the Helstrom bound is `1/2` plus a quarter of the state distance.
declarations.statement:
lemma optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq (ω₀ ω₁ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    optimalSuccessProb ω₀ ω₁ ⟨1 / 2, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩ = 1 / 2 + dist ω₀ ω₁ / 4

modules.title: States of a local net
modules.doc:
Compatible subsystem states and states of the whole system.

## i. Overview

An observable of a smaller subsystem can also be measured in a larger one. A state of the larger
subsystem therefore determines a state of the smaller one: assign each smaller observable the
expectation it has when viewed in the larger system. This operation is called restriction.
Observable inclusions point from smaller to larger subsystems, state restrictions point the other
way.

In a tensor product system, including an observable means letting it act as the identity on the
additional factors. Restricting a density-matrix state then amounts to tracing out those factors.
A `LocalNet.CompatibleStates` assigns a state to every subsystem, with the requirement that a
smaller subsystem's state agrees with the restriction of any larger subsystem's state. Thus the
expectation of an observable does not depend on which containing subsystem is used to evaluate
it.

For a nonempty directed family, local positivity defines an order on the quasilocal observables.
Every compatible family then defines a unique state of the whole system. Conversely, a quasilocal
state restricts to a compatible family of subsystem states.

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet.restrict`: precomposition with the observable inclusion map.
- `LocalNet.CompatibleStates`: a compatible family of states on the subsystems.
- `LocalNet.CompatibleStates.compat_apply`: compatible states agree on included observables.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.toState`: the quasilocal state defined by a compatible family.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal.stateEquiv`: quasilocal states correspond to compatible local states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Restriction of states
- B. Compatible local states
- C. States of the whole system

## iv. References

sections.text:
## B. Compatible local states

A compatible family assigns a state to every local subsystem. Whenever one subsystem is contained
in another, its state must agree with the restriction of the larger subsystem's state. This
ensures that local observables have consistent expectation values, even in infinite systems with
correlations and entanglement.

## C. States of the whole system

A quasilocal observable has a local representative. A compatible family evaluates that
representative in its subsystem; compatibility makes the result independent of the representative.

declarations.doc: Restrict a state of `Y` to `X` by pulling it back along the observable inclusion channel.

lemma restrict_apply (h : X ≤ Y) (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, A Y]) (a : A X) :

declarations.statement: lemma restrict_refl (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, A X]) : N.restrict (le_refl X) ω = ω

modules.title: The metric space of states
modules.doc:
The operator-norm distance between states and their distance to the set of pure states.

## i. Overview

A state is just a positive linear functional — no continuity is assumed. It turns out to be
automatically bounded: `|ω A| ≤ ‖A‖`. Physically, a state can never predict
an expectation value bigger than what the observable itself can read.

That bound induces a genuine operator-norm distance between states, `dist`, making `𝓢[ℝ, E]` a
`MetricSpace`. It also defines `distToPure`, the infimum distance to the set of pure states.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm` : a state's values are bounded by the
  order-unit norm.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist` : the operator-norm distance between states.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.distToPure` : a state's infimum distance to the set of pure states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. States are bounded by the order-unit norm
- B. The state metric
- C. Distance to pure states

## iv. References

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_le_one
declarations.doc: A state takes values at most `1` on observables bounded by the unit.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_le_one {F : Type*} [OrderUnitSpace F] (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, F]) {A : F} (hA : A ≤ 1) :
    ω A ≤ 1

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_le_orderUnitNorm
declarations.doc: A state never overshoots the order-unit norm.
declarations.statement: lemma apply_le_orderUnitNorm (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (A : E) : ω A ≤ orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm
declarations.doc: A state's values are bounded by the order-unit norm in both directions.
declarations.statement: lemma abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (A : E) : |ω A| ≤ orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.abs_apply_sub_apply_le_two
declarations.doc:
Two states' predictions on any observable of order-unit norm at most `1` never differ by more
than `2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma abs_apply_sub_apply_le_two (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) {A : E} (hA : orderUnitNorm A ≤ 1) :
    |ω A - φ A| ≤ 2

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_bddAbove
declarations.doc:
The values `|ω A - φ A|` of two states, restricted to the order-unit-norm unit ball, are
bounded by `2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_bddAbove (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun A : {A : E // orderUnitNorm A ≤ 1} => |ω A - φ A|)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.instNonemptyOrderUnitBall
declarations.statement: instance instNonemptyOrderUnitBall : Nonempty {A : E // orderUnitNorm A ≤ 1}

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist
declarations.doc:
The operator-norm distance between two states: how far apart their predictions can get on an
observable of order-unit norm at most `1`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def dist (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : ℝ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_nonneg
declarations.doc: Distances between states are nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_nonneg (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : 0 ≤ dist ω φ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_le_two
declarations.doc: The whole state space has diameter at most `2`: it's a bounded metric space.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_le_two (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : dist ω φ ≤ 2

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_self
declarations.statement: lemma dist_self (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : dist ω ω = 0

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_comm
declarations.doc: The state distance is symmetric.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_comm (ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : dist ω φ = dist φ ω

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.dist_triangle
declarations.doc: The state distance satisfies the triangle inequality.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_triangle (ω φ ψ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : dist ω ψ ≤ dist ω φ + dist φ ψ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.eq_of_dist_eq_zero
declarations.doc: `dist` separates states: two states at distance `0` are equal.
declarations.statement: lemma eq_of_dist_eq_zero {ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]} (h : dist ω φ = 0) : ω = φ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_effectEquiv
declarations.doc:
A state's value at a doubled, re-centered effect (`effectEquiv`) is twice its value at
the effect, minus one.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_effectEquiv (ψ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (e : Effect E) :
    ψ (effectEquiv e) = 2 * ψ e - 1

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.instMetricSpace
declarations.doc: States, metrized by the operator norm induced by the order-unit norm on `E`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable instance instMetricSpace : MetricSpace (𝓢[ℝ, E])

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.distToPure
declarations.doc: The infimum distance to the set of pure states, using `Metric.infDist`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def distToPure (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : ℝ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.distToPure_nonneg
declarations.doc: The distance to the set of pure states is nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma distToPure_nonneg (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : 0 ≤ distToPure ω

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.distToPure_eq_zero_of_isPure
declarations.doc: A pure state is at distance `0` from the set of pure states.
declarations.statement: lemma distToPure_eq_zero_of_isPure {ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]} (h : IsPure ω) : distToPure ω = 0

modules.title: The state–effect pairing
modules.doc:
State–effect evaluation gives probabilities and separates both states and effects.

## i. Overview

States and effects are paired by evaluation, `(ω, e) ↦ ω e ∈ [0, 1]`. This pairing is affine in
both arguments. It also separates both spaces: a state is determined by its values on all
effects, and an effect is determined by its values under all states. Moreover, the distance
between two effects is the largest difference in probability that they can produce over all
states.

Thus states and effects admit faithful representations as probability-valued functions on one
another.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_mem_Icc` : state–effect evaluation takes values in `[0, 1]`.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_mix` : evaluation is affine in the effect argument.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ext_of_effect_eq` : effects separate states.
- `Effect.dist_eq_sSup_abs_apply` : effect distance is determined by state evaluations.
- `Effect.ext_of_forall_apply_eq` : states separate effects.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.injective_apply_effect` : states embed into functions on effects.
- `Effect.injective_apply_state` : effects embed into functions on states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. State–effect evaluation
- B. Effects separate states
- C. States separate effects

## iv. References

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_mem_Icc
declarations.doc: State–effect evaluation takes values in `[0, 1]`.
declarations.statement: lemma apply_mem_Icc (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (e : Effect E) : ω e ∈ Set.Icc 0 1

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_mix
declarations.doc: Evaluation is affine in the effect argument.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_mix (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (e f : Effect E) (t : unitInterval) :
    ω (Effect.mix e f t) = (t : ℝ) * ω e + (1 - (t : ℝ)) * ω f

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ext_of_effect_eq_of_nonneg
declarations.doc: Two states that agree on all effects agree on every nonnegative element.
declarations.statement:
lemma ext_of_effect_eq_of_nonneg {ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]}
    (h : ∀ e : Effect E, ω e = φ e) {B : E} (hB : 0 ≤ B) : ω B = φ B

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ext_of_effect_eq
declarations.doc: A state is determined by its values on effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma ext_of_effect_eq {ω φ : 𝓢[ℝ, E]}
    (h : ∀ e : Effect E, ω e = φ e) : ω = φ

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.injective_apply_effect
declarations.doc: Evaluation on effects is injective on states.
declarations.statement:
lemma injective_apply_effect :
    Function.Injective (fun (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (e : Effect E) => ω e)

declarations.name: Effect.dist_eq_sSup_abs_apply
declarations.doc:
The distance between two effects is the supremum of the difference in their evaluations over
all states.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_eq_sSup_abs_apply [Nontrivial E] (e f : Effect E) :
    Dist.dist e f = sSup (Set.range fun ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E] => |ω e - ω f|)

declarations.name: Effect.ext_of_forall_apply_eq
declarations.doc: An effect is determined by its values under all states.
declarations.statement:
lemma ext_of_forall_apply_eq {e f : Effect E}
    (h : ∀ ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E], ω e = ω f) : e = f

declarations.name: Effect.injective_apply_state
declarations.doc: Evaluation by states is injective on effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma injective_apply_state :
    Function.Injective (fun (e : Effect E) (ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) => ω e)

modules.title: Separation by states
modules.doc:
States determine positivity, the order-unit norm, and equality of observables.

## i. Overview

In an Archimedean order-unit space, states determine the entire ordered normed structure. An
element is positive exactly when every state assigns it a nonnegative value, and its order-unit
norm is `‖A‖₁ = sup { |ω A| : ω a state }`. Consequently, states separate points: two elements are
equal whenever every state assigns them the same value.

The main ingredient is Hahn–Banach separation of a point from the positive cone. Applied to an
element `A ≱ 0`, it produces a state `ω` with `ω A < 0`. Everything else follows from this one
separation fact.

## ii. Key results

- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.exists_apply_neg_of_not_nonneg` : every element outside the positive
  cone is separated from it by a state.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.nonneg_iff_forall_state_nonneg` : states determine the positive cone.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.sSup_abs_apply_eq_orderUnitNorm` : states determine the order-unit norm.
- `UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ext_of_forall_apply_eq` : states separate points.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Separating points from the cone
- B. The positive cone
- C. The order-unit norm
- D. Separation of points

## iv. References

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.apply_eq_zero_of_apply_one_eq_zero
declarations.doc: A positive functional vanishing at the order unit vanishes everywhere.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_eq_zero_of_apply_one_eq_zero [OrderUnitSpace E] {p : E →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ}
    (h1 : p (1 : E) = 0) (A : E) : p A = 0

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.exists_apply_neg_of_not_nonneg
declarations.doc: Every element outside the positive cone is strictly separated from it by a state.
declarations.statement: lemma exists_apply_neg_of_not_nonneg {A : E} (hA : ¬ 0 ≤ A) : ∃ ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E], ω A < 0

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.nonneg_iff_forall_state_nonneg
declarations.doc: An element is positive iff every state assigns it a nonnegative value.
declarations.statement: lemma nonneg_iff_forall_state_nonneg (A : E) : 0 ≤ A ↔ ∀ ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E], 0 ≤ ω A

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.instNonemptyState
declarations.doc: Every nontrivial Archimedean order-unit space has a state.
declarations.statement: instance instNonemptyState [Nontrivial E] : Nonempty (𝓢[ℝ, E])

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.orderUnitNorm_le_iff_forall_abs_apply_le
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is at most `r` iff every state predicts an absolute value at most `r`.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_le_iff_forall_abs_apply_le [Nontrivial E] (A : E) (r : ℝ) :
    orderUnitNorm A ≤ r ↔ ∀ ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E], |ω A| ≤ r

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.sSup_abs_apply_eq_orderUnitNorm
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is the supremum of `|ω A|` over all states `ω`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sSup_abs_apply_eq_orderUnitNorm [Nontrivial E] (A : E) :
    sSup (Set.range fun ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E] => |ω A|) = orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.orderUnitNorm_one
declarations.doc: The order unit has norm exactly `1`.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_one [Nontrivial E] : orderUnitNorm (1 : E) = 1

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.ext_of_forall_apply_eq
declarations.doc: States separate points: if `ω A = ω B` for every state `ω`, then `A = B`.
declarations.statement: lemma ext_of_forall_apply_eq {A B : E} (h : ∀ ω : 𝓢[ℝ, E], ω A = ω B) : A = B

modules.title: Equivalence between states and finite normalized weights
modules.doc:
Finite normalized weights correspond exactly to positive unital linear functionals.

## i. Overview

A state is, on its own terms, a normalized positive linear functional — `𝓢[ℝ, E]`, already fully
built in `State/Basic.lean`. It is not *defined* as a weight; the two are independent notions, and
the correspondence between them is a genuine theorem.

## ii. Key results

- `Weight.stateEquiv` : finite normalized weights correspond exactly to states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. From a normalized weight to a state
- B. From a state to a weight
- C. The equivalence

## iv. References

## B. From a state to a weight

declarations.doc: A finite normalized weight extends to a state.

declarations.doc: The extended state agrees with the weight on positive observables.
declarations.statement: lemma toState_apply (hw : w.IsState) (A : PosCone E) : hw.toState A = (w A).toReal

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toWeight
declarations.doc:
The weight induced by a state: `ENNReal.ofReal` applied to the state's values on the positive
cone, where they are automatically nonnegative.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def toWeight (s : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : Weight E

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toWeight_apply
declarations.statement: lemma toWeight_apply (s : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (A : PosCone E) : s.toWeight A = ENNReal.ofReal (s (A : E))

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toReal_toWeight_apply
declarations.doc: The weight induced by a state agrees with the state itself on the positive cone.
declarations.statement:
lemma toReal_toWeight_apply (s : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) (A : PosCone E) :
    (s.toWeight A).toReal = s (A : E)

declarations.name: UnitalPositiveLinearMap.toWeight_isState
declarations.doc: The weight induced by a state is finite and normalized.
declarations.statement: lemma toWeight_isState (s : 𝓢[ℝ, E]) : s.toWeight.IsState

declarations.name: Weight.stateEquiv
declarations.doc: Finite normalized weights correspond exactly to states.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def stateEquiv : {w : Weight E // w.IsState} ≃ 𝓢[ℝ, E]

modules.title: Weights
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

A state assigns each positive observable a nonnegative expectation value, normalized so the
certain outcome reads exactly `1`. A *weight* generalizes this by dropping the normalization and
letting the values be extended nonnegative reals, possibly `+∞`. This matters especially in
infinite dimensions: the trace on `B(H)` is only finite on the trace-class operators and genuinely
diverges to `+∞` elsewhere. A state is then the special case that happens to be finite everywhere
and normalized.

## ii. Key results

- `Weight.monotone` : weights are monotone on the positive cone.
- `Weight.IsFinite.isSemifinite` : a finite weight is automatically semifinite.
- `Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isState` : rescaling a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit
  turns it into a state.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Weights
- B. States as weights

## iv. References

- G. Ludwig, *Foundations of Quantum Mechanics I*, Springer, 1983.
  <https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-86751-4>

declarations.name: Weight
declarations.doc: An extended nonnegative linear functional on the positive cone.
declarations.statement: abbrev Weight (E : Type*) [OrderedVectorSpace E]

declarations.name: Weight.IsFaithful
declarations.doc: Only the zero positive element has weight zero.
declarations.statement: def IsFaithful (w : Weight E) : Prop

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite
declarations.doc: A weight has no infinite values.
declarations.statement: def IsFinite (w : Weight E) : Prop

declarations.name: Weight.IsSemifinite
declarations.doc: A weight is the supremum of its finite values below each positive element.
declarations.statement: def IsSemifinite (w : Weight E) : Prop

declarations.name: Weight.monotone
declarations.doc: Weights are monotone on the positive cone.
declarations.statement: lemma monotone (w : Weight E) : Monotone w

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.isSemifinite
declarations.doc: A finite weight is semifinite.
declarations.statement: lemma IsFinite.isSemifinite {w : Weight E} (hw : w.IsFinite) : w.IsSemifinite

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toReal_map_add
declarations.doc: A finite weight's real value is additive.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.toReal_map_add {w : Weight E} (hw : w.IsFinite) (A B : PosCone E) :
    (w (A + B)).toReal = (w A).toReal + (w B).toReal

declarations.name: Weight.toReal_map_nnreal_smul
declarations.doc: A weight's real value scales linearly under nonnegative real scaling.
declarations.statement:
lemma toReal_map_nnreal_smul (w : Weight E) (k : ℝ≥0) (A : PosCone E) :
    (w (k • A)).toReal = k * (w A).toReal

declarations.name: Weight.IsNormal
declarations.doc:
A weight is normal when it preserves least upper bounds of increasing sequences in the
positive cone.
declarations.statement: def IsNormal (w : Weight E) : Prop

declarations.name: Weight.IsState
declarations.doc: A weight that's finite everywhere and gives the certain outcome weight exactly `1`.
declarations.statement:
structure IsState (w : Weight E) : Prop where
  /-- A state is finite everywhere. -/
  finite : w.IsFinite
  /-- A state gives the certain outcome weight exactly `1`. -/
  normalized : w 1 = 1

declarations.name: Weight.normalize
declarations.doc: Rescale a weight by the inverse of its value at the order unit.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def normalize (w : Weight E) : Weight E

declarations.name: Weight.normalize_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma normalize_apply (w : Weight E) (A : PosCone E) :
    normalize w A = (w 1)⁻¹ * w A

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isFinite
declarations.doc: Normalizing a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit keeps it finite.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.normalize_isFinite {w : Weight E} (hw : w.IsFinite) (h : w 1 ≠ 0) :
    (normalize w).IsFinite

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isState
declarations.doc:
Normalizing a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit makes it a state: the order unit
is scaled to weight exactly `1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.normalize_isState {w : Weight E} (hw : w.IsFinite) (h : w 1 ≠ 0) :
    (normalize w).IsState

modules.title: Extending finite weights
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

An `ℝ≥0`-linear map on the positive cone extends uniquely to an `ℝ`-linear map on the whole space
as soon as every element is a difference `P - Q` of positive elements: send `P - Q` to
`f P - f Q`. In an order-unit space every element is such a difference, so a finite weight extends
to a positive linear functional.

## ii. Key results

- `PosCone.extend` : the `ℝ`-linear extension of an `ℝ≥0`-linear map on the positive cone.
- `Weight.IsFinite.toLinearMap` : the `ℝ`-linear map extending a finite weight to all of `E`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Extension from the positive cone
- B. Extending finite weights

## iv. References

declarations.name: PosCone.coe_nnreal_smul
declarations.statement: lemma coe_nnreal_smul (t : ℝ≥0) (P : PosCone E) : ((t • P : PosCone E) : E) = (t : ℝ) • (P : E)

declarations.name: PosCone.map_sub_eq_map_sub
declarations.doc: `P - Q ↦ f P - f Q` does not depend on how an element is written as a difference.
declarations.statement:
lemma map_sub_eq_map_sub {P Q P' Q' : PosCone E} (h : (P : E) - Q = P' - Q') :
    f P - f Q = f P' - f Q'

declarations.name: PosCone.exists_sub
declarations.doc: In an order unit space, every element is a difference of positive elements.
declarations.statement: lemma exists_sub (A : E) : ∃ P Q : PosCone E, (P : E) - Q = A

declarations.name: PosCone.extendFun
declarations.doc: The value of the extension, computed from a chosen decomposition `A = P - Q`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def extendFun (A : E) : ℝ

declarations.name: PosCone.extendFun_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma extendFun_eq {A : E} {P Q : PosCone E} (h : (P : E) - Q = A) :
    extendFun f A = f P - f Q

declarations.name: PosCone.extend
declarations.doc: The `ℝ`-linear extension of an `ℝ≥0`-linear map on an order unit space's positive cone.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def extend : E →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: PosCone.extend_apply
declarations.statement: lemma extend_apply {P Q : PosCone E} : extend f ((P : E) - Q) = f P - f Q

declarations.name: PosCone.extend_coe
declarations.statement: lemma extend_coe (P : PosCone E) : extend f (P : E) = f P

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toReal
declarations.doc: A finite weight, read as a real-valued `ℝ≥0`-linear map on the positive cone.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def IsFinite.toReal (hw : w.IsFinite) : PosCone E →ₗ[ℝ≥0] ℝ

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toReal_apply
declarations.statement: lemma IsFinite.toReal_apply (hw : w.IsFinite) (A : PosCone E) : hw.toReal A = (w A).toReal

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toLinearMap
declarations.doc: The `ℝ`-linear map extending a finite weight.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def IsFinite.toLinearMap (hw : w.IsFinite) : E →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toLinearMap_coe
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.toLinearMap_coe (hw : w.IsFinite) (A : PosCone E) :
    hw.toLinearMap (A : E) = (w A).toReal
